articles.title: Chinese-owned science journal created to rival the best
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02759-zNewly-launched Vita is part of a broader government plan to give China a bigger say in what counts as high quality science.
articles.content:
Vita is a new international open-access journal based in China.Credit: Michael Szebor/Nature

A new Chinese-owned journal has set its sights on rivalling the world’s oldest and most influential academic titles. Vita is one of several English-language journals that have launched in China in the past couple of years. They represent the country’s latest effort to create prestigious global journals, as part of the government’s Journal Excellence Action Plan, which began in 2019.

Until recently, institutes and universities in China have often worked with international publishing companies to run English journals. “What sets Vita apart is that it is a completely Chinese journal, launched by Chinese scientists and published by a Chinese publisher,” says Ning Zhang, founder of TopEdit, a company based in Gaithersburg, Maryland, that helps Chinese journals to build global presence.

China is a global leader in scientific research, but only a small portion of that research is published in Chinese-owned journals.

China views establishing its own journals as a way to raise its presence in the global scientific community, says Chen Fuyou, director of XinRui Journal Ranking, an independent journal evaluation website, based in Beijing. “This means China would get to define what is a high-quality paper and what is high-quality research, based on its own measures and selection processes. It would also get to decide what papers to publish,” Chen says.

Free publishing

Vita is jointly funded by the Higher Education Press, a subsidiary of China’s Ministry of Education based in Beijing, and Westlake University in Hangzhou, its editorial team says. It publishes papers in biological sciences. Its first print issue came out in July.

As an open-access journal, Vita waives article-processing charges (APCs), fees many publishers require authors to pay when publishing open access articles.

The high cost to researchers in China of paying APCs to international publishers — US$909 million in 2024 — is another reason why China wants to establish its own journals. Since March, the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) has stopped funding the APCs of 30 of the most expensive open-access journals.

Vita’s model is “clearly going to be appealing” to authors, says James Butcher, a former publisher who runs a consultancy firm called Journalology near Liverpool, UK. But he warns that keeping the model running in the long term will be a challenge for the journal and its funders because “publishing is expensive”. Publishers who charge APCs say that the money helps to cover the costs of publishing open access, including paying the salaries of in-house editors and production staff, as well as printing and server costs.

But whether Vita’s funders will be willing to foot the APC bills indefinitely for a large volume of foreign authors is an open question, says Butcher. “If there are 20% or 30% of papers coming from the United States, for example, is that something they would be happy to bankroll?”

Vita says that it is committed to not charging APCs to international researchers no matter the volume of submissions.

Big financial support

As part of its plan to build globally influential journals, China’s government offers generous financial support to four-hundred and fifty homegrown journals; for example, some English-language journals can receive up to 1.5 million yuan (roughly $223,000) per year for five years.

The plan also supports 13 Chinese academic organizations that publish journals. “The government’s goal is to help these companies to grow into major academic publishing groups, like Springer Nature. This is deemed a more efficient way than cultivating individual journals,” Zhang says.

Going global
articles.reasoning: The article describes the launch of a new Chinese-owned international open-access scientific journal, Vita, which aims to rival established global journals. This represents a significant development in global scientific publishing, increasing accessibility by waiving article-processing charges and allowing China to contribute more prominently to defining high-quality research. The initiative has broad implications for the global scientific community and research dissemination.

articles.title: How to put people first in cyberspace
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02960-0Digital technologies increasingly shape everyday life. Computer scientist Francine Berman tells Nature that stronger safeguards are required to protect the public interest.
articles.content:
Better Tech: Putting People First in Cyberspace Francine Berman MIT Press (2026)

For decades, computer scientist Francine Berman has helped to shape the digital world. In Better Tech, the University of Massachusetts Amherst scholar makes the case that technology should serve the public interest. It is a timely manifesto for how to put people’s welfare at the centre of discussions about technological progress.

You argue that digital technologies are essential infrastructure, yet often lack safeguards. Could you elaborate?

Rules to keep AI in check: nations carve different paths for tech regulation

When we think about critical infrastructure such as roads, the electrical grid and the financial system, we expect safeguards to protect the public. Those protections are a long way from being perfect. Bridges collapse, power grids fail and financial crises happen. But we still invest heavily in oversight, safety measures and regulation because these systems underpin everyday life.

Digital technologies now have a similarly central role, yet we often treat them differently. Instead of assuming they should be trustworthy and well governed, we spend a great deal of time protecting ourselves from them and questioning whether we can trust them. If we began treating digital technologies as critical infrastructure, we would be more likely to build them with safety, reliability and public benefit in mind from the outset. That would mean stronger standards and clearer rules about how these technologies are developed and used. The goal is not to eliminate risk, but to take these essential technologies seriously enough to manage that risk well.

Do search engines and social-media platforms count as critical infrastructure?

I think search engines crossed that threshold long ago. Once most information moved online, such searches became the main way that people found knowledge and made decisions. In that sense, search engines are infrastructure. We need food to sustain our bodies; and we need reliable information to sustain an informed society. The problem is that today’s information systems are governed mostly by business incentives. Search engines use algorithms that connect users with advertisers, often prioritizing content on the basis of commercial interests rather than public benefit. That does not mean that they are inherently harmful, but it does mean that their influence is too important to operate without greater transparency and accountability.

The same is true of social media. Many of the most important public announcements, political debates and cultural conversations now happen there. What was once communicated through press releases or by official institutions is increasingly communicated through social platforms. They have become essential channels for public life. Yet these platforms often lack the safeguards that we would expect from infrastructure of that importance. Users face cyberbullying and predatory behaviour. Recommendation systems can pull people into endless scrolling and narrow information environments. None of this is inevitable. These platforms were designed to maximize growth and engagement, and they have been remarkably successful at doing that. But design choices are choices. We could build systems that are both profitable and protective.

Treating digital technologies as critical infrastructure could lead to better regulation.Credit: Olivier Douliery/AFP/Getty

Are social-media firms taking accountability for alleged harm to users, or avoiding the issue?

Perhaps a bit of both. For example, the company Meta has come to a financial settlement with some US states that claimed its products harmed child safety. But it’s worth remembering that the firm faces various legal and regulatory challenges, so the significance of any one settlement depends on how it fits into that broader landscape. One positive development, however, is that people are increasingly demanding accountability from technology companies. What interests me most about these court cases is not the financial penalties, but the product changes Meta might be required to make. The meaningful question is whether the court settlements lead to a product redesign that reduces addictive features or gives users more control.

The changes that have been publicly announced do not go far enough. Although these are small steps, I think the fact that we are starting to hold these companies accountable means that they’re more likely to create better products in the future, which is really what we want.

Do you think, like social-media firms, artificial-intelligence companies are now designing systems that can be addictive?

I think it’s important to distinguish between AI and the products that use it. AI is a broad field. In their 2021 textbook Artificial Intelligence, computer scientists Stuart Russell and Peter Norvig describe AI along two dimensions: whether a system is designed to think or to act, and whether it aims to behave like a human or like a rational agent. That creates four broad categories of AI research. These give rise to distinct research questions, and they continue to be active areas of AI development. Unfortunately, in popular discourse, AI has become a broad umbrella term, making it harder to distinguish between applications that are genuinely useful and those that are not.

What AI risks do you think we’re paying too much and, conversely, too little attention to?

Will AI ruin the social sciences — or revolutionize them?

There are genuine risks when people start treating AI systems as if they have human qualities. We’ve seen troubling cases, especially involving young people, in which individuals have turned to chatbots for companionship and received poor or even harmful advice. In some instances, the consequences have been tragic. Those risks deserve attention.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a significant and timely call for stronger safeguards and accountability in digital technologies, emphasizing their role as critical infrastructure that impacts society broadly. It focuses on the need for better regulation and design choices that prioritize public welfare over commercial interests, which has meaningful implications for millions of users worldwide.
articles.personality_title: Putting people first: Making digital technology safer and fairer
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Digital technology like search engines and social media now play a central role in everyday life. But unlike roads or electricity, these technologies often lack rules to protect people from harm or unfair practices.

**What happened** – Computer scientist Francine Berman wrote a book called Better Tech, arguing that digital tools should be treated like critical infrastructure. This means they need strong safeguards, clear rules, and designs that focus on public welfare, not just business profit. Berman points out that search engines and social media are already essential for finding information and sharing ideas, so they should be made safer and more trustworthy.

**Impact** – Treating digital technology as critical infrastructure is important because it can reduce risks like harmful content, cyberbullying, and addictive designs. It also pushes companies to be more transparent and accountable. For example, some social media firms have faced legal challenges over child safety, leading to small product changes. Berman believes these efforts, though limited now, can grow into better protections for users worldwide.

**What's next step** – The next step involves stronger regulation and redesign of digital platforms to manage risks better. Courts and public pressure could encourage companies to create safer, more user-friendly products. There is also a need to clearly understand different types of artificial intelligence to focus on real problems, such as harmful chatbot interactions, and avoid unnecessary fears.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Digital technologies must be treated like essential infrastructure with strong safeguards to protect people and support a healthier online world.
articles.personality_title_fr: Mettre les gens au premier plan : rendre la technologie numérique plus sûre et plus juste
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La technologie numérique, comme les moteurs de recherche et les réseaux sociaux, joue aujourd’hui un rôle central dans la vie quotidienne. Mais contrairement aux routes ou à l’électricité, ces technologies manquent souvent de règles pour protéger les gens contre les risques ou les pratiques injustes.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – La scientifique en informatique Francine Berman a écrit un livre intitulé Better Tech, dans lequel elle soutient que les outils numériques doivent être considérés comme des infrastructures critiques. Cela signifie qu’ils doivent bénéficier de protections solides, de règles claires et d’un design centré sur le bien public, pas seulement sur le profit commercial. Berman souligne que les moteurs de recherche et les réseaux sociaux sont déjà essentiels pour trouver des informations et partager des idées, ils doivent donc être rendus plus sûrs et plus fiables.

**Impact** – Traiter la technologie numérique comme une infrastructure critique est important car cela peut réduire les risques tels que les contenus nuisibles, le cyberharcèlement et les conceptions addictives. Cela pousse aussi les entreprises à plus de transparence et de responsabilité. Par exemple, certaines plateformes sociales ont dû faire face à des défis juridiques liés à la sécurité des enfants, ce qui a entraîné de petits changements de produits. Berman pense que ces efforts, bien que limités pour l’instant, peuvent devenir de meilleures protections pour les utilisateurs dans le monde entier.

**Prochaines étapes** – La prochaine étape est une réglementation plus forte et une refonte des plateformes numériques pour mieux gérer les risques. Les tribunaux et la pression publique pourraient encourager les entreprises à créer des produits plus sûrs et plus adaptés aux utilisateurs. Il est aussi nécessaire de mieux comprendre les différents types d’intelligence artificielle pour se concentrer sur les vrais problèmes, comme les interactions nuisibles avec les chatbots, et éviter les peurs inutiles.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les technologies numériques doivent être traitées comme des infrastructures essentielles avec des protections solides pour protéger les personnes et favoriser un monde en ligne plus sain.
articles.personality_title_es: Poner a las personas primero: hacer la tecnología digital más segura y justa
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La tecnología digital como los motores de búsqueda y las redes sociales ahora juegan un papel central en la vida diaria. Pero a diferencia de las carreteras o la electricidad, estas tecnologías a menudo carecen de reglas para proteger a las personas de daños o prácticas injustas.

**Qué pasó** – La científica informática Francine Berman escribió un libro llamado Better Tech, donde sostiene que las herramientas digitales deben tratarse como infraestructura crítica. Esto significa que necesitan fuertes protecciones, reglas claras y diseños que se enfoquen en el bienestar público, no solo en las ganancias comerciales. Berman señala que los motores de búsqueda y las redes sociales ya son esenciales para encontrar información y compartir ideas, por lo que deben hacerse más seguros y confiables.

**Impacto** – Tratar la tecnología digital como infraestructura crítica es importante porque puede reducir riesgos como contenido dañino, ciberacoso y diseños adictivos. También impulsa a las empresas a ser más transparentes y responsables. Por ejemplo, algunas redes sociales enfrentaron desafíos legales por la seguridad infantil, lo que llevó a pequeños cambios en sus productos. Berman cree que estos esfuerzos, aunque limitados ahora, pueden convertirse en mejores protecciones para usuarios en todo el mundo.

**Próximo paso** – El siguiente paso incluye una regulación más fuerte y rediseño de las plataformas digitales para manejar mejor los riesgos. Los tribunales y la presión pública podrían motivar a las empresas a crear productos más seguros y amigables. También es necesario entender claramente los diferentes tipos de inteligencia artificial para enfocarse en problemas reales, como interacciones dañinas con chatbots, y evitar miedos innecesarios.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Las tecnologías digitales deben tratarse como infraestructura esencial con fuertes protecciones para cuidar a las personas y apoyar un mundo en línea más saludable.

articles.title: OpenAI unveils AI assistant 'dots' while safety worries delay new model
articles.summary: Sam Altman spoke in San Francisco during OpenAI’s annual event for tech developers.
articles.content:
OpenAI on Tuesday unveiled "dots", a new artificial intelligence (AI) assistant it says can proactively carry out tasks on a user's behalf.

At its annual developer day in San Francisco, chief executive Sam Altman referred to "dots" as "remarkably capable, always-on agents that can handle really anything you can think of."

At the same time, OpenAI president Greg Brockman and other tech leaders held a meeting with President Donald Trump as the firm faces intense scrutiny after internal tests of its AI agents revealed unexpected and occasionally harmful actions.

Dots, however, were pitched as brightly coloured cute cartoons meant to function as digital assistants for people with busy lives.

The dots, Altman said, "can handle really anything you can think of."

A glossy video was shown during the event, with people speaking to and naming animated versions of their "dots," then giving them various tasks, like building a website and booking afterschool activities for their children.

Speaking about "my dot," Altman almost entirely eschewed referring to the tool as an agent, which has been in common use for years. AI agents are essentially AI chatbots that are programmed to operate somewhat autonomously.

"You just give your dot a responsibility... and your dots will just get to work and keep working," Altman added.

At the event, Altman reiterated his decision for OpenAI to not make a highly anticipated stock market debut until it can "make confident safety decisions".

The company has been preparing for a blockbuster listing, potentially valuing the firm at up to $1.4tn (£1.06tn).

Altman told reporters that "it is going to take us some time to figure out how to make sure that alignment, monitoring, safety, security stay well ahead of capabilities."

OpenAI's event on Tuesday took place as President Donald Trump held a White House lunch with tech leaders and House Speaker Mike Johnson.

Trump repeated his belief that AI companies should regulate themselves.

He also said they had discussed creating a ten-person committee to oversee the sector, adding there would be "tremendous self-policing"

Some researchers and company heads have called for a slowdown in AI development as more instances of breaches by AI firms' models become public.

"We need to navigate the centrist path," Altman told the BBC during a question and answer session with reporters on Tuesday.

"I am hopeful that the industry will figure out a more sensible, more pragmatic stance than has been exhibited by some of the members of our industry," he added, declining to specify particular company names or leaders.

The day prior to OpenAI's event, the company said it was delaying the launch of its latest model due to certain safety issues that showed up during internal testing.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on OpenAI unveiling a new AI assistant 'dots' designed to proactively assist users, which represents a significant technological innovation with broad potential impact. The focus on safety and responsible deployment highlights a positive approach to AI development, addressing public concerns and aiming for beneficial societal use. The story is detailed and centered on this single technological advancement and its implications.
